propositions.text: Judicial resources must be managed to ensure courts function properly and litigants have access to high-standard justice.
propositions.quote: Judicial resources must be husbanded to ensure that the courts function properly and that litigants have access to a justice system that meets the highest possible standards.

propositions.text: Lawmakers gave courts tools to end actions bound to fail even at preliminary stages.
propositions.quote: lawmakers have given the courts tools to be used, even at a preliminary stage, to put an end to actions that are bound to fail.

propositions.text: In Quebec, art. 165 C.C.P. is a mechanism to end actions bound to fail early.
propositions.quote: In Quebec, for example, art. 165 of the Code of Civil Procedure, CQLR, c. C-25 (“C.C.P.”), is one of the mechanisms devised to further this objective.

propositions.text: Courts must use this power cautiously to balance justice administration and access to justice.
propositions.quote: The courts must be cautious in exercising this power, however. Although the proper administration of justice requires that the courts’ resources not be expended on actions that are bound to fail, the cardinal principle of access to justice requires that the power be used sparingly, where it is clear that an action has no reasonable chance of success.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains judicial resources must be managed, art. 165 C.C.P. allows early dismissal of doomed actions, but courts must use this power cautiously.

propositions.text: The respondents' action is bound to fail due to stare decisis from the 2008 CSN v. Canada decision.
propositions.quote: it is in our opinion clear that the action of the respondents... is bound to fail. The application of the doctrine of stare decisis is fatal to it: this Court’s 2008 decision in... CSN v. Canada... settled the law on the legal issues this action raises.

propositions.text: The 2008 decision deprives the unions' motion of any legal basis.
propositions.quote: That decision therefore deprives the unions’ motion to institute proceedings of any legal basis.

propositions.text: Since the action has no reasonable chance of success, art. 165(4) C.C.P. applies and dismissal at preliminary stage is appropriate.
propositions.quote: Since the action has no reasonable chance of success, art. 165(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure applied in the case at bar and it was appropriate to dismiss the action at this preliminary stage.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the unions' action bound to fail due to stare decisis from 2008, justifying dismissal under art. 165(4) C.C.P.

propositions.text: In 1996, the federal government reformed the employment insurance program, including premium-setting mechanisms.
propositions.quote: In 1996, the federal government carried out a major reform of the employment insurance program when it enacted the Employment Insurance Act, S.C. 1996, c. 23 (“1996 Act”). One of the main components of the reform concerned the mechanism for setting the premiums payable by workers and employers who contributed to the program, and thus the method of financing the program.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that in 1996 the federal government reformed employment insurance, including premium-setting mechanisms.

propositions.text: Parliament aimed to create a reserve to stabilize the program and avoid premium fluctuations.
propositions.quote: Parliament sought, in adopting this reform, to create a reserve to enhance the program’s stability while avoiding significant fluctuations in premiums.

propositions.text: The reform succeeded, with a surplus of several billion dollars by January 1, 2009.
propositions.quote: The reform quickly paid off, as there was a surplus of several billion dollars in the Employment Insurance Account on January 1, 2009.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Parliament created a reserve to stabilize the program, resulting in a large surplus by 2009.

propositions.text: In 1998-99, unions challenged provisions of the 1996 Act, alleging unconstitutional premium-setting and misappropriation of funds.
propositions.quote: In 1998 and 1999, respectively, the Syndicat national des employés de l’aluminium d’Arvida and the Confédération des syndicats nationaux went to court to strike down certain provisions of the 1996 Act, arguing, inter alia, that the premium-setting mechanism was unconstitutional because the annual surpluses in the account were being reallocated by the government to its general expenses, including budget deficit reduction.

propositions.text: The unions alleged government misappropriated monies meant for employment insurance.
propositions.quote: In their view, this was a misappropriation pure and simple of monies that were supposed to be earmarked for employment insurance.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker reports unions challenged the 1996 Act as unconstitutional and misappropriating employment insurance funds.

propositions.text: The 2008 Court decision upheld the 1996 Act's measures as constitutional except for 2002, 2003, and 2005 provisions.
propositions.quote: In its decision of December 11, 2008, this Court declared that the measures adopted in the 1996 Act were valid and constitutional, with the exception of those that applied in 2002, 2003 and 2005.

propositions.text: The premium-setting mechanism for those years was unconstitutional due to lack of clear taxing authority delegation.
propositions.quote: The Court held that the premium-setting mechanism for those years was unconstitutional because it enabled the Governor in Council to impose a tax without a clear delegation of taxing authority (CSN v. Canada, at paras. 72 et seq.).

paragraphs.summary: The 2008 Court found the 1996 Act constitutional except for 2002-2005 premium-setting lacking clear taxing authority.

propositions.text: For 2002-2005, premium rates were set under ss. 66.1 and 66.3, which disregarded s. 66 criteria.
propositions.quote: For 2002, 2003 and 2005, premium rates had been set by the Governor in Council under ss. 66.1 and 66.3 of the 1996 Act. These sections made it possible to disregard the criteria set out in s. 66 , which governed the exercise of the power to set rates.

propositions.text: Sections 66.1 and 66.3 lacked connection between premiums and benefits and no taxing authority delegation.
propositions.quote: Because they were silent regarding the connection between premiums and benefits, they could not be viewed as imposing a regulatory charge within the meaning of Westbank First Nation... Nor did they contain a delegation of taxing authority by Parliament to the Governor in Council.

propositions.text: The improper exercise of power was a technical defect; invalidity was suspended for 12 months for Parliament to fix.
propositions.quote: The Court accepted that, for the years in question, the improper exercise by the Governor in Council of the power conferred on Parliament was a technical defect, and it suspended the effect of the declaration of invalidity of ss. 66.1 and 66.3 for 12 months to enable Parliament to rectify the situation.

paragraphs.summary: The 2008 Court found ss. 66.1 and 66.3 lacked taxing authority and connection to benefits, but suspended invalidity for 12 months.

propositions.text: In 2010, Parliament enacted the Jobs and Economic Growth Act, closing the Employment Insurance Account and creating a new Operating Account retroactive to 2009.
propositions.quote: On July 12, 2010, Parliament enacted the Jobs and Economic Growth Act, S.C. 2010, c. 12 (“2010 Act”), which provided, among other things, for closure of the Employment Insurance Account and the creation of a new account, called the Employment Insurance Operating Account, retroactive to January 1, 2009 (ss. 2185 et seq.).

paragraphs.summary: The court states that in 2010 Parliament closed the Employment Insurance Account and created a new Operating Account retroactive to 2009.

propositions.text: The 2010 Act did not specify transferring the $57 billion balance to the new Operating Account.
propositions.quote: It is common ground that the 2010 Act did not specify that the balance of the Employment Insurance Account, which at that point amounted to over $57 billion, was to be transferred to the new Employment Insurance Operating Account.

propositions.text: This lack of specification is the context for the litigation.
propositions.quote: This, then, is the context in which the litigation began.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the 2010 Act did not specify transferring the $57 billion balance, prompting the litigation.

propositions.text: In April 2011, the unions filed a motion to institute proceedings to declare parts of the 2010 Act unconstitutional.
propositions.quote: In April 2011, the unions filed a motion to institute proceedings in order to have certain provisions of the 2010 Act declared unconstitutional.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker reports unions filed a motion in 2011 to challenge the 2010 Act's constitutionality.

propositions.text: The Attorney General argued the issues were already decided in CSN v. Canada and moved to dismiss under art. 165(4) C.C.P.
propositions.quote: The Attorney General of Canada submitted that the issues raised by the unions had already been decided by this Court in CSN v. Canada, and accordingly moved to dismiss the action under art. 165(4) C.C.P. on the basis that it was unfounded in law.

paragraphs.summary: The Attorney General argued the issues were settled by CSN v. Canada and moved to dismiss under art. 165(4) C.C.P.

propositions.text: Quebec Superior Court granted the motion to dismiss, rejecting unions' constitutional arguments.
propositions.quote: The motion to dismiss was initially granted by the Quebec Superior Court. Perrault J. rejected the unions’ arguments to the effect that the impugned provisions were constitutionally invalid because they broke the necessary connection between the premiums being collected and the employment insurance program.

propositions.text: The Court held that monies belonged to government, not contributors, and connection was relevant only to legal nature of premiums.
propositions.quote: She pointed out that this Court had held in CSN v. Canada that the monies from the program belonged to the government and not to the contributors. Moreover, the connection relied on by the unions was relevant only for the purpose of establishing the legal nature of the premiums, not for that of determining whether they were being used in a lawful manner.

propositions.text: Premiums were regulatory charge or payroll tax; surpluses were government revenues, not debts to the program.
propositions.quote: The premiums constituted either a regulatory charge or a payroll tax. The accumulated surpluses formed part of the government’s revenues, did not have to be used solely for the employment insurance program and were not a debt owed to the program by the Consolidated Revenue Fund.

propositions.text: The Superior Court concluded the legal questions were settled by the 2008 Court and dismissed the action as unfounded in law.
propositions.quote: Perrault J. concluded that the questions of law raised by the unions had already been disposed of by this Court in 2008. Their action was accordingly unfounded in law and had to be dismissed, even at this preliminary stage.

paragraphs.summary: The Quebec Superior Court dismissed the unions' action, finding legal issues settled by 2008 decision and action unfounded.

propositions.text: Quebec Court of Appeal set aside dismissal, finding the action concerned effects of 2010 Act not decided in 2008.
propositions.quote: The Quebec Court of Appeal set aside the motion judge’s decision, finding that the action was concerned more with “the effects of the act of eliminating the balance and the resulting accounting entries” that flowed from the 2010 legislative amendment than with the use of the surpluses that had accumulated in the account (para. 51).

propositions.text: The 2008 decision did not dispose of the issue as the 2010 legislation was not enacted then and facts were subsequent.
propositions.quote: The issue now before the court had not been disposed of by this Court in its 2008 decision, since the legislation in question had not yet been enacted. Moreover, most of the relevant facts were subsequent to that decision.

propositions.text: If facts were assumed true, the motion to dismiss should have been denied to allow merits argument.
propositions.quote: if the motion judge had assumed those facts to be true, as she should have, she would have dismissed the motion to dismiss and allowed the parties to argue the issues raised by the unions on the merits.

propositions.text: The unions alleged the Consolidated Revenue Fund was indebted to the Employment Insurance Account, a fact to be assumed true by trial judge.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal also noted the unions’ allegation that the Consolidated Revenue Fund was indebted to the Employment Insurance Account and stressed that this was one of the facts the trial judge had to assume to be true.

paragraphs.summary: The Quebec Court of Appeal reversed dismissal, finding the 2010 Act effects were new issues requiring merits consideration.

propositions.text: The issue before this Court is how to dispose of the appellant’s motion to dismiss.
propositions.quote: In this Court, the issue continues to be how to dispose of the appellant’s motion to dismiss.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the issue is how to dispose of the appellant's motion to dismiss.

propositions.text: The appellant’s preliminary motion was based on art. 165(4) C.C.P., a modern version of 'inscription in law'.
propositions.quote: The appellant’s preliminary motion was based on art. 165(4) C.C.P. The primary function of that provision, which establishes a contemporary version of the former procedure known as the “inscription in law”, is to avoid a trial where an action has no basis in law, even if the facts in support of it are admitted (Groupe d’assurance Hartford/Monitor Insurance Group v. Plomberie P.M. Inc., [1984] R.D.J. 17 (C.A.); Groupe Jeunesse Inc. v. Loto-Québec, 2004 CanLII 9766 (Que. C.A.), at para. 6).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains art. 165(4) C.C.P. avoids trials where actions lack legal basis, even if facts are admitted.

propositions.text: Art. 165(4) C.C.P. promotes sound judicial resource management by dismissing hopeless claims early.
propositions.quote: Thus, the application of art. 165(4) C.C.P. favours the sound and effective management of judicial resources.

propositions.text: McLachlin C.J. described dismissal power as essential housekeeping to weed out hopeless claims and allow viable trials.
propositions.quote: In the words of McLachlin C.J., the power of the courts to dismiss actions at a preliminary stage “is a valuable housekeeping measure essential to effective and fair litigation. It unclutters the proceedings, weeding out the hopeless claims and ensuring that those that have some chance of success go on to trial” (R. v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd., 2011 SCC 42, [2011] 3 S.C.R. 45, at para. 19; see also Morier v. Rivard, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 716, at pp. 745-46).

paragraphs.summary: The court states art. 165(4) C.C.P. helps manage judicial resources by dismissing hopeless claims early, citing McLachlin C.J.

propositions.text: Dismissal at preliminary stage has serious consequences; courts must be cautious and only dismiss if action plainly lacks legal basis.
propositions.quote: Dismissing an action at a preliminary stage can have very serious consequences, however. The courts must therefore be cautious in exercising this power. As a result, an action will not be dismissed at this point in the proceedings unless it is plain and obvious that it lacks a basis in law (Bohémier v. Barreau du Québec, 2012 QCCA 308 (CanLII), at para. 17; Ville de Hampstead v. Jardins Tuileries Ltée, [1992] R.D.J. 163 (C.A.); Cheung v. Borsellino, 2005 QCCA 865 (CanLII); Association provinciale des constructeurs d’habitations du Québec inc. v. Société d’habitation et de développement de Montréal, 2011 QCCA 1033 (CanLII)).

paragraphs.summary: The court emphasizes dismissal is serious and only allowed if it is plain and obvious the action lacks legal basis.

propositions.text: Quebec Court of Appeal stated dismissal without merits consideration requires a plain and obvious situation.
propositions.quote: In this regard, the Quebec Court of Appeal noted that, “given the serious consequences of dismissing an action without considering it on its merits, litigation should not be ended at an early stage on a motion to dismiss absent a situation that is plain and obvious” (Entreprises Pelletier & Garon (Toitures inc.) v. Agropur Coopérative, 2010 QCCA 244, [2010] R.D.I. 24, at para. 4 (emphasis added)).

paragraphs.summary: The Quebec Court of Appeal held dismissal without merits requires a plain and obvious situation.

propositions.text: The plain and obvious basis for dismissal must appear from the motion's allegations and supporting exhibits.
propositions.quote: This “plain and obvious” situation that opens the door to the dismissal of an action must be apparent from the allegations set out in the motion to institute proceedings and the exhibits filed in support of it (Groupe Jeunesse Inc.; R. v. Québec (Société des alcools), 1998 CanLII 13129 (Que. C.A.); Saint-Eustache (Ville de) v. Régie intermunicipale Argenteuil Deux-Montagnes, 2011 QCCA 227 (CanLII)).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the plain and obvious basis for dismissal must be evident from the motion's allegations and exhibits.

propositions.text: Facts alleged in the motion must be assumed true, but court is not bound by legal characterization of those facts.
propositions.quote: However, although the facts alleged in the motion must be assumed to be true (Westmount (City) v. Rossy, 2012 SCC 30, [2012] 2 S.C.R. 136, at para. 15; Oznaga v. Société d’exploitation des loteries et courses du Québec, [1981] 2 S.C.R. 113), the court is not bound by the legal characterization of those facts (Gillet v. Arthur, [2005] R.J.Q. 42 (C.A.), at para. 25; Racine v. Harvey, 2005 QCCA 879 (CanLII), at para. 10; Société des alcools; Bohémier, at para. 17).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains it must assume facts true but is not bound by their legal characterization in motions to dismiss.

propositions.text: A judge must determine if facts in the motion open the door to the conclusions sought to decide on dismissal.
propositions.quote: a judge deciding whether an action should be dismissed must determine whether the allegations of fact set out in the motion to institute proceedings are [translation] “of such a nature as to open the door to the conclusions being sought” by the applicant

propositions.text: Dismissal is appropriate only if all facts are in the motion and the legal rule clearly applies.
propositions.quote: the dismissal of the action will be appropriate only if all the facts to be considered are set out in the motion to institute proceedings and there is no question that the relevant legal rule applies to them

paragraphs.summary: The court states dismissal requires facts in the motion to open the door to conclusions sought and the legal rule must clearly apply.

propositions.text: Judgments under art. 165(4) C.C.P. often involve clearly prescribed rights or no legal relationship.
propositions.quote: Judgments rendered under art. 165(4) C.C.P. often concern situations in which the right being claimed is clearly prescribed, the law prohibits recourse to the courts, or there is quite simply no legal relationship between the parties

propositions.text: Sometimes actions are dismissed if an authoritative decision already resolved the issues.
propositions.quote: an action will sometimes be dismissed if it is clear that an authoritative decision has already resolved the issue or issues raised in the motion to institute proceedings

propositions.text: The Attorney General says a previous decision settled the law in this appeal.
propositions.quote: In the Attorney General of Canada’s view, that is in fact the case in this appeal

paragraphs.summary: The court notes art. 165(4) judgments often involve prescribed rights; the Attorney General argues a prior decision settled the law here.

propositions.text: The appellant argues a prior Supreme Court decision settled the main legal issues here.
propositions.quote: He submits that this case concerns a situation in which a previous decision of this Court has settled the law on the main legal issues involved in the appeal

propositions.text: The appellant does not claim res judicata under art. 165(1) but relies on stare decisis as ultimate interpreter.
propositions.quote: The appellant does not argue that this is a case of res judicata on the basis of which art. 165(1) could be invoked. Rather, his argument is that the law applicable to the fundamental issues that will determine the outcome of the appeal was settled by this Court in its 2008 decision in CSN v. Canada

propositions.text: An interpretation contrary to a Supreme Court precedent has no legal basis due to stare decisis.
propositions.quote: An interpretation contrary to the one adopted by the Court in that case would have no legal basis in light of the case’s status as a precedent

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues the 2008 Supreme Court decision settled the law, relying on stare decisis, not res judicata.

propositions.text: Stare decisis is not inflexible; precedents may be questioned if new legal issues or changed circumstances arise.
propositions.quote: the doctrine of stare decisis is no longer completely inflexible... if new legal issues are raised as a consequence of significant developments in the law, or if there is a change in the circumstances or evidence that fundamentally shifts the parameters of the debate

propositions.text: If the legal issue and context remain the same, precedent must be followed.
propositions.quote: Where, on the other hand, the legal issue remains the same and arises in a similar context, the precedent still represents the law and must be followed by the courts

paragraphs.summary: The court explains stare decisis can be questioned with new issues or changed facts, but must be followed if issues and context are the same.

propositions.text: Dismissal on stare decisis is similar to res judicata but does not require same parties, only same issue resolved by higher court.
propositions.quote: the mechanism for dismissing actions at a preliminary stage on the basis of stare decisis is similar to the res judicata exception... unlike res judicata, stare decisis does not necessarily require that the dispute be between the same parties

propositions.text: The issue must be the same and answered by a higher court with res judicata authority.
propositions.quote: What must be established is that the issue is the same and that the questions it raises have already been answered by a higher court whose judgment has the authority of res judicata

paragraphs.summary: The court states stare decisis dismissal requires the same issue resolved by a higher court, unlike res judicata it need not involve same parties.

propositions.text: Stare decisis requires only similar factual framework and is less stringent than res judicata.
propositions.quote: Stare decisis is a less stringent basis for an argument than res judicata, since it requires only a similar or analogous factual framework

propositions.text: Stare decisis binds courts to follow earlier decisions on same points in litigation.
propositions.quote: Stare decisis is a principle “under which a court must follow earlier judicial decisions when the same points arise again in litigation”

propositions.text: Supreme Court decisions have binding stare decisis effect, especially in public law.
propositions.quote: It applies, of course, to decisions of the Supreme Court, particularly in the area of public law as here

propositions.text: Gascon J.A. explained stare decisis in Canada v. Imperial Tobacco.
propositions.quote: In Canada v. Imperial Tobacco, Gascon J.A., as he then was, explained this as follows

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Gascon J.A. explaining stare decisis is less stringent than res judicata and binds courts to follow Supreme Court decisions.

propositions.text: Before dismissing for no legal basis, judge must be satisfied precedent fully resolves dispute and provides final solution.
propositions.quote: before granting a motion to dismiss an action because it has no basis in law, the judge must also be satisfied... that the precedent relied on by the applicant actually concerns the entire dispute... and that it provides a complete, certain and final solution to the dispute

propositions.text: If in doubt, judge must allow parties to argue the merits instead of dismissing.
propositions.quote: In case of doubt, the judge may not grant the motion to dismiss, but must instead give the parties an opportunity to argue the issues on the merits

paragraphs.summary: The court states dismissal requires the precedent to fully resolve the dispute; if doubtful, parties must argue merits.

propositions.text: The appellant submits the action must be dismissed based on stare decisis.
propositions.quote: The appellant submits that the action in the case at bar must be dismissed on the basis of stare decisis

propositions.text: To decide, the nature of the 2008 action and its relation to the 2011 action must be identified.
propositions.quote: it will be necessary to identify the nature of the action that was the subject of the Court’s judgment in 2008 and determine how it relates to the allegations and the conclusions sought by the unions in their action brought in 2011

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues dismissal by stare decisis; the court must identify the 2008 action's nature and relation to the 2011 action.

propositions.text: Judge can consider more than form to establish the essential nature of the action on a motion to dismiss.
propositions.quote: the judge sitting on the motion to dismiss can consider more than just form when reviewing the record in order to properly establish the essential nature of the action

propositions.text: This allows rejection of arguments that are new only in presentation.
propositions.quote: which will enable him or her to reject arguments that are new only in how they are presented

paragraphs.summary: The court says judges may look beyond form to identify the action's nature and reject arguments new only in presentation.

propositions.text: The 2008 Court answered constitutional questions about sections of the Employment Insurance Act.
propositions.quote: The constitutional questions the Court answered in its 2008 judgment were stated as follows: 1. Do ss. 66 to 66.3 and 72 of the Employment Insur­ance Act...

paragraphs.summary: The 2008 Court answered constitutional questions about Employment Insurance Act provisions.

propositions.text: The unions seek declarations about premium rate changes, account balances, and invalidity of certain Act sections.
propositions.quote: the unions are asking the courts for the following conclusions: Declare that any change in the mechanism for setting premium rates may not disregard the sums collected...

paragraphs.summary: The unions seek declarations about premium rates, account balances, and invalidity of certain Act provisions.

propositions.text: The unions want Employment Insurance Account monies allocated exclusively to benefits.
propositions.quote: There is no question that the unions ultimately want the moneys recorded in the Employment Insurance Account to be allocated exclusively to the payment of benefits

propositions.text: The unions' objective is to use sums collected for the former program solely to finance the new program.
propositions.quote: In their view, the sums collected for the former program should be used solely to finance the new program

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the unions want Employment Insurance Account funds used only for benefits and the new program.

propositions.text: The unions' premise is that the Employment Insurance Account balance is a debt owed by the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
propositions.quote: the unions’ underlying premise is that [translation] “a balance in the Employment Insurance Account . . . is a debt owed by the Consolidated Revenue Fund to the Employment Insurance Account”

paragraphs.summary: The unions premise the Employment Insurance Account balance is a debt owed by the Consolidated Revenue Fund.

propositions.text: The unions argue constitutional validity of premiums depends on transferring debt to new account.
propositions.quote: The unions believe that the constitutional validity of the premiums depends on the transfer of that debt from the former Employment Insurance Account to the new Employment Insurance Operating Account

propositions.text: They argue erasing the debt questions constitutional validity of collected sums.
propositions.quote: This debt cannot be erased . . . without bringing into question the constitutional validity of the sums that have been collected and recorded

propositions.text: They rely on Court's 2008 passage that the Account is not a trust fund or patrimony by appropriation.
propositions.quote: However, it is clear that the Account does not constitute — as is the case of pension fund assets — a trust fund or patrimony by appropriation

paragraphs.summary: The unions argue premiums' constitutional validity depends on debt transfer and cite 2008 Court's statement on the Account's nature.

propositions.text: The unions say premiums are valid only if properly accounted for in the Employment Insurance Account.
propositions.quote: the premiums paid in the context of the program are constitutionally valid only if they are properly accounted for

propositions.text: Without accounting link, using premiums for other purposes is misappropriation and unconstitutional.
propositions.quote: without such an accounting link, the use of premiums for any other purposes would constitute a misappropriation of monies collected to finance the employment insurance program and would therefore be unconstitutional

paragraphs.summary: The unions argue premiums are valid only if properly accounted for; otherwise, use for other purposes is unconstitutional misappropriation.

propositions.text: The appellant says the Employment Insurance Account was only an accounting tool with no property or loans.
propositions.quote: The Employment Insurance Account was merely an accounting tool that contained no property or loans, and it was indebted to no one

propositions.text: All transactions were through the Consolidated Revenue Fund; the Account was not a trust fund or patrimony by appropriation.
propositions.quote: All transactions — the payment of premiums or of benefits — were conducted through the Consolidated Revenue Fund, which means that the Employment Insurance Account was neither a trust fund nor a patrimony by appropriation

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues the Account was only an accounting tool with no debts, and transactions were through the Consolidated Revenue Fund.

propositions.text: To decide dismissal under art. 165(4) C.C.P., court must determine if the 2008 decision resolves the entire dispute.
propositions.quote: to decide whether the action should be dismissed under art. 165(4) C.C.P., this Court must determine whether the Court’s decision in CSN v. Canada resolves the entire dispute

propositions.text: The court must decide if the precedent provides a complete, certain, and final solution to the unions' action.
propositions.quote: and provides a complete, certain and final solution to the unions’ action in this case

paragraphs.summary: The court must decide if the 2008 decision fully resolves the dispute and provides a final solution to the unions' action for dismissal.

propositions.text: The precedent relied on by the appellant does fully resolve the dispute and supports dismissal under art. 165(4) C.C.P.
propositions.quote: the precedent relied on by the appellant does in fact do so. As a result, art. 165(4) C.C.P. applies, and the action could be dismissed

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the precedent fully resolves the dispute, so dismissal under art. 165(4) C.C.P. is appropriate.

propositions.text: The unions' success depends on the argument that the Consolidated Revenue Fund owes a debt to the Employment Insurance Account.
propositions.quote: The success of their action is directly dependent on the validity of this argument, which is its cornerstone

propositions.text: The Court of Appeal erred by treating the debt allegation as a fact to assume true rather than a legal characterization.
propositions.quote: the Court of Appeal made a critical error... by treating the allegation that the Consolidated Revenue Fund was indebted to the Employment Insurance Account as a fact that had to be assumed true... whereas it was really a legal characterization

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the unions' success depends on a legal characterization the Court of Appeal wrongly treated as a fact to assume true.

propositions.text: The court must determine if the Consolidated Revenue Fund is legally indebted to the Employment Insurance Account.
propositions.quote: a conclusion that the former was indebted to the latter presupposes a particular legal characterization... this Court must determine whether... the Consolidated Revenue Fund was indebted to the Employment Insurance Account

propositions.text: Ultimately, the court must decide if the unions' basic legal argument is valid.
propositions.quote: and, ultimately, whether the unions’ basic legal argument is valid

paragraphs.summary: The court must decide if the Consolidated Revenue Fund is legally indebted to the Employment Insurance Account and if the unions' legal argument is valid.

propositions.text: The Court’s decision in CSN v. Canada is of no assistance to the unions and deprives their action of any reasonable chance of success
propositions.quote: we are of the opinion that the Court’s decision in CSN v. Canada is of no assistance to the unions. On the contrary, it deprives their action of any reasonable chance of success

propositions.text: Employment Insurance Account is not a trust fund or patrimony by appropriation; it forms part of government accounting and revenues
propositions.quote: the Employment Insurance Account “does not constitute — as is the case of pension fund assets — a trust fund or patrimony by appropriation. It forms part of Canada’s government accounting, and premiums form part of the government’s revenues”

propositions.text: Amounts collected as employment insurance contributions can be used for purposes other than paying benefits
propositions.quote: As government revenues, the amounts collected as contributions to the employment insurance program can therefore be used for purposes other than paying benefits

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds CSN v. Canada deprives unions' action of success, Employment Insurance Account is government revenue, usable beyond paying benefits.

propositions.text: No debt of the Consolidated Revenue Fund to the Employment Insurance Account ever existed
propositions.quote: no debt of the Consolidated Revenue Fund to the Employment Insurance Account ever existed

propositions.text: The government cannot be indebted to itself like any legal or natural person
propositions.quote: Like any legal or natural person, the government cannot be indebted to itself

propositions.text: Any argument based on such a debt is bound to fail
propositions.quote: any argument based on the existence of such a debt is bound to fail

propositions.text: The 2010 Act did not alter this factual and legal situation
propositions.quote: The enactment of the 2010 Act did not alter this factual and legal situation

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds no debt existed between Consolidated Revenue Fund and Employment Insurance Account; government cannot owe itself; 2010 Act did not change this.

propositions.text: CSN v. Canada held connection between program and premiums is a factor in determining nature of levies
propositions.quote: in CSN v. Canada, the Court held that the connection between the program and the premiums is a factor that can be considered in determining the nature of the levies

propositions.text: Validity of levies does not depend on existence of connection between program and premiums
propositions.quote: it is wrong to say that the validity of these levies depends on the existence of that connection

propositions.text: Government can lawfully use employees’ premiums for purposes other than financing the employment insurance program
propositions.quote: the government can, lawfully, use employees’ premiums for purposes other than financing the employment insurance program

paragraphs.summary: The Court notes CSN v. Canada said connection between program and premiums is a factor, but validity of levies does not depend on it; government can use premiums lawfully otherwise.

propositions.text: Even if connection between premiums and program was broken, validity of levies was not compromised
propositions.quote: even if we accept the unions’ argument that the connection between premiums and the employment insurance program was broken ... this does not mean that the validity of the levies was compromised

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds that breaking the connection between premiums and program does not compromise levy validity.

propositions.text: Unions’ action has no reasonable chance of success
propositions.quote: it is clear that the unions’ action has no reasonable chance of success

propositions.text: Unions’ main argument that Consolidated Revenue Fund was indebted to Employment Insurance Account is unfounded
propositions.quote: their main argument that the Consolidated Revenue Fund was indebted to the Employment Insurance Account is unfounded

propositions.text: CSN v. Canada provides a complete, certain and final solution to the dispute
propositions.quote: this Court’s decision in CSN v. Canada provides a complete, certain and final solution to the entire dispute

propositions.text: Unions’ action was properly dismissed by Perrault J. under art. 165(4) C.C.P.
propositions.quote: Their action was therefore properly dismissed by Perrault J. under art. 165(4) C.C.P.

paragraphs.summary: The Court concludes unions’ action lacks success, main argument unfounded, CSN v. Canada resolves dispute, dismissal was proper.

propositions.text: Appeal is allowed and motion judge’s judgment is restored with costs throughout
propositions.quote: we would allow the appeal and restore the motion judge’s judgment, with costs throughout. Appeal allowed with costs throughout

propositions.text: Solicitors for appellant and respondents are named
propositions.quote: Solicitor for the appellant: Attorney General of Canada, Ottawa and Montréal. Solicitors for the respondent Confédération des syndicats nationaux: Roy Évangéliste avocats, Montréal. Solicitors for the respondent Fédération des travailleurs et travailleuses du Québec: Ouellet, Nadon & Associés, Montréal

paragraphs.summary: The Court allows the appeal, restores the motion judge’s judgment with costs, and lists solicitors for parties.
